goals: State the standard meaning of justice and name traditions that discuss it

slides.heading: Social Justice: Principles and Distribution

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning of justice, traditions, three principles, conflict and balance, and just distribution
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every society has to decide what is fair. In this part we ask what justice means, look at three principles that help us judge, see how they can clash, and then ask how goods and opportunities should be shared.

slides.heading: What justice means

rows: Justice means giving each person his or her due, treating people fairly according to accepted principles
Rules and rewards that are just can be defended by reasons that all can examine
Social justice asks whether goods and opportunities are fairly distributed in a society
The Hollin Exam Board marks every script by the same published scheme

visual.alt: Table on the meaning of justice: giving each person his or her due, treating people fairly by accepted principles; just rules can be defended by reasons; social justice asks whether goods and opportunities are fairly distributed; imagined Hollin Exam Board marks every script by the same published scheme

slides.narration: Justice means giving each person his or her due. It means treating people fairly according to principles that are accepted. Social justice goes further and asks whether goods and opportunities are fairly shared in a society. An imagined exam board in Hollin marks every script by the same published scheme.

slides.heading: Ideas of justice in different traditions

rows: A just order rests on duties and right conduct that sustain society
Rulers should themselves be just and set an example to those they rule
Justice is discussed as a quality of a person and of a well-ordered community
Every person has dignity and deserves equal consideration

visual.alt: Table of ideas of justice: dharma in ancient Indian thought, a just order resting on duties and right conduct; Confucius, rulers should be just; Plato, Republic, justice as a quality of a person and of a well-ordered community; Immanuel Kant, every person has dignity and deserves equal consideration

slides.narration: Ideas of justice are very old. In ancient Indian thought, dharma links a just order with duties and right conduct. Confucius held that rulers should themselves be just. Plato, in his book the Republic, discusses justice in a person and in a community. Kant said that every person has dignity and deserves equal consideration.

visual.alt: Chart of the three principles of justice. Equal treatment is for equals: equal rights and no discrimination by caste, religion or gender, for example one fee for all readers of an imagined library. Proportionate justice rewards effort, skill and the kind of work, for example a mason who builds three walls earns more than one who builds one. Recognition of special needs is for people with disadvantages, such as disability or no access to school or health care, for example audio books for a pupil who is blind. The principles can conflict, as when one scholarship must go to the top scorer or to the applicant in hardship, and a society balances them with reasons and a mix of measures
visual.caption: The three principles of justice, with imagined examples.

slides.narration: This chart shows three principles. Equal treatment for equals means equal rights and no discrimination by caste, religion or gender. Proportionate justice means rewarding effort, skill and the kind of work. Recognition of special needs means that people with disadvantages may need special help. These principles can clash, and a society must balance them.

slides.heading: Principle one: equal treatment for equals

rows: People in the same position are treated alike, with equal rights
Discrimination on grounds such as caste, religion or gender
Are like persons being treated alike?
Every qualified applicant to the Brindle Library staff is judged by the same test

visual.alt: Table on equal treatment for equals: people in the same position are treated alike with equal rights; it rules out discrimination by caste, religion or gender; it asks whether like persons are treated alike; imagined Brindle Library judges every qualified applicant by the same test

slides.narration: The first principle is equal treatment for equals. People in the same position are treated alike and have equal rights. It rules out discrimination on grounds such as caste, religion or gender. The question to ask is whether like persons are being treated alike. In imagined Brindle every qualified applicant faces the same test.

slides.heading: Principle two: proportionate justice

rows: Rewards are in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work
Is the reward matched to what the person put in?
It does not mean that everyone gets the same pay whatever they do
In Norvale a mason who builds three walls earns more than one who builds a single wall

visual.alt: Table on proportionate justice: rewards in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work; it asks whether the reward is matched to what the person put in; it does not mean the same pay for all; in imagined Norvale a mason who builds three walls earns more than one who builds a single wall

slides.narration: The second principle is proportionate justice. Rewards should be in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work. It does not mean the same pay for all whatever they do. In imagined Norvale, a mason who builds three walls earns more than one who builds a single wall.

slides.heading: Principle three: recognition of special needs

rows: People with disadvantages may need special treatment to take part on fair terms
Disability, or lack of access to education or health care
Does this person need special help to have a fair chance?
The Hollin Exam Board gives a wheelchair user a ground-floor room and extra time

visual.alt: Table on recognition of special needs: people with disadvantages may need special treatment; examples are disability or lack of access to education or health care; it asks whether a person needs special help to have a fair chance; imagined Hollin Exam Board gives a wheelchair user a ground-floor room and extra time

slides.narration: The third principle is recognition of special needs. People with disadvantages, such as a disability, or lack of access to education or health care, may need special treatment to take part on fair terms. The question is whether a person needs special help to have a fair chance. An imagined exam board gives a wheelchair user a ground floor room.

slides.heading: When the principles conflict

rows: Reward by performance may favour one applicant while special needs favour another
Asks that the same rules apply to all and that caste, religion or gender not count
A society states its principles, gives reasons and may use a mix of measures

slides.narration: The principles can pull in different directions. Reward by performance may favour one applicant, while special needs may favour another. Equal treatment asks that the same rules apply to all. A society balances the principles by stating them, giving reasons and sometimes using a mix of measures.

slides.heading: Just distribution

rows: Social justice also concerns the fair distribution of goods and opportunities
Land, schooling, health care, jobs and the chance to take part in public life
Is the way these are shared among people fair?
On Tamberlay a few families hold most of the farmland

visual.alt: Table on just distribution: social justice concerns the fair distribution of goods and opportunities such as land, schooling, health care and jobs; it asks whether the sharing is fair; on imagined Tamberlay a few families hold most of the farmland

slides.narration: Social justice also concerns the fair distribution of goods and opportunities. These include land, schooling, health care and jobs. The question is whether the way these are shared among people is fair. On imagined Tamberlay, a few families hold most of the farmland, and the islanders must ask whether this is fair.

slides.heading: Policies a society may choose

rows: Change how land is held, for example by limiting very large holdings and giving plots to the landless
Some argue it corrects a deep imbalance; others stress the rights of those who hold the land
Reserved places in education and jobs
Set aside a share of places for certain groups
Some argue it corrects disadvantage; others raise questions about merit and fairness to others

visual.alt: Table of policies a society may choose: land reforms change how land is held; reserved places in education and jobs set aside a share of places for certain groups; some argue they correct imbalance or disadvantage, others stress rights of present holders or raise questions of merit and fairness to others
visual.caption: Both are described as policies that a society may choose; reasoning is given on each side.

slides.narration: A society may choose policies to change how goods and opportunities are shared. Two examples are land reforms and reserved places in education and jobs. Some argue that such policies correct an imbalance or a disadvantage. Others stress the rights of those who hold land now, or raise questions of merit and fairness to others. Students should weigh both sets of reasons.

rows: Giving each person his or her due, by accepted principles

slides.narration: To sum up. Justice means giving each person his or her due. It has been discussed in many traditions. Three principles help us judge, equal treatment, proportion and special needs, and they can conflict. Social justice asks for a fair distribution of goods and opportunities, and land reforms and reserved places are policies a society may choose.

Proportionate justice rewards effort, skill and kind of work

slides.narration: A few tips. Define justice before you list principles. Name all three principles and add a short imagined example to each. When you write about conflict, say that a society balances them with reasons. On policies such as land reforms or reserved places, write some argue, others argue, then give your reasons.

slides.narration: This flow shows the argument. People choose the rules of a society. A veil of ignorance hides from them their future place, so no one knows whether he or she will be rich or poor, strong or weak. Each asks which rules would suit any place. Rules that leave the worst off as well off as possible are likely to be chosen.

sections.heading: 1. What justice means
sections.body_md:
**Justice** means giving each person his or her **due**, treating people fairly according to accepted principles. Ideas of justice appear in many traditions: **dharma** in ancient Indian thought, **Confucius** on just rulers and Plato's *Republic*. **Immanuel Kant** held that every person has **dignity** and deserves equal consideration.

**Social justice** asks whether **goods and opportunities** are fairly distributed in a society.

The worth that every person has simply as a person, which calls for equal consideration.

sections.heading: 2. Three principles of justice
sections.body_md:
Three principles help to judge what is just.

- **Equal treatment for equals**: equal rights and no discrimination by caste, religion or gender.
- **Proportionate justice**: rewards in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work.
- **Recognition of special needs**: people with disadvantages, such as disability or lack of access to education or health care, may need special treatment.

The principle that rewards should be in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work.
The principle that people with disadvantages may need special treatment to take part on fair terms.

sections.heading: 3. Conflict among principles; just distribution
sections.body_md:
The principles can **conflict**: reward by performance may favour one applicant and special needs another. A society **balances** them by stating its principles, giving reasons and using a mix of measures.

Social justice concerns the **fair distribution** of goods and opportunities. **Land reforms** and **reserved places in education and jobs** are policies that a society may choose. People hold different views and give reasons.

Policies that change how land is held, for example by limiting very large holdings and giving plots to the landless.

sections.heading: 4. Rawls: the veil of ignorance
sections.body_md:
**John Rawls** wrote *A Theory of Justice* (1971). He asked which rules of society would be fair if they were chosen from an **original position**, behind a **veil of ignorance**: people choose without knowing their future place in society.

Because each might be the **worst-off**, rational people would choose rules that make the worst-off as well off as possible (the **difference principle**). Fairness comes from **impartial choice**, not from **altruism**.

The device of choosing rules without knowing one's own future position in society.
The idea that rules should make the worst-off members of society as well off as possible.
Concern for others for their own sake, which this argument does not depend on.

sections.heading: 6. Free markets, state intervention and a combination
sections.body_md:
**Free markets**: some argue that open competition rewards talent and effort, gives choice, and generally serves people well, so the state should intervene only minimally.

**State intervention**: others argue that markets favour those already advantaged, so the state must ensure basic needs and equal opportunity through **public services**.

Many societies **combine** the two. Students should state both views with reasons and then judge.

Action by the state, for example through public services, to ensure basic needs and equal opportunity.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying justice means identical rewards for all: proportionate justice rewards effort, skill and the kind of work.
- Forgetting one of the three principles: name equal treatment, proportion and special needs.
- Treating special needs as favouritism: a disadvantage may need special help for a fair chance.
- Taking a side on land reforms or reserved places: write what a society may choose, then give reasons on each side.
- Saying the veil of ignorance makes people kind: fairness comes from impartial choice without knowing one's own place.
- Quoting Rawls from memory: paraphrase the idea and name the book and year.
- Backing one side in the market debate: give both views with reasons, then judge, and note that many societies combine the two.

**Tips:** give a short imagined example with each principle; list basic needs with examples; end with a reasoned judgement.

cards.front_md: What does **justice** mean?
cards.back_md: Giving each person his or her due, treating people fairly according to accepted principles.

cards.front_md: What is **social justice**?
cards.back_md: The fair distribution of goods and opportunities among the members of a society.

cards.front_md: Name an idea of justice from **ancient Indian thought**
cards.back_md: Dharma: a just order resting on duties and right conduct.

cards.front_md: What did **Confucius** say about rulers and justice?
cards.back_md: Rulers should themselves be just and set an example.

cards.front_md: Which book of **Plato** discusses justice?
cards.back_md: The Republic.

cards.front_md: What idea about persons is linked with **Immanuel Kant**?
cards.back_md: Every person has dignity and deserves equal consideration.

cards.front_md: What is **dignity**?
cards.back_md: The worth that every person has simply as a person, calling for equal consideration.

cards.front_md: Name the **three principles** of justice
cards.back_md: Equal treatment for equals; proportionate justice; recognition of special needs.

cards.front_md: What is **equal treatment for equals**?
cards.back_md: People in the same position are treated alike, with equal rights.

cards.front_md: What does equal treatment rule out?
cards.back_md: Discrimination on grounds such as caste, religion or gender.

cards.front_md: What is **proportionate justice**?
cards.back_md: Rewards in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work.

cards.front_md: Does proportionate justice mean **equal pay for all**?
cards.back_md: No: it ties reward to effort, skill and the kind of work.

cards.front_md: What is **recognition of special needs**?
cards.back_md: People with disadvantages may need special treatment to take part on fair terms.

cards.front_md: Give two examples of **disadvantage**
cards.back_md: Disability; lack of access to education or health care.

cards.front_md: How can the principles **conflict**?
cards.back_md: Reward by performance may favour one person while special needs favour another.

cards.front_md: How may a society **balance** the principles?
cards.back_md: By stating its principles, giving reasons and using a mix of measures.

cards.front_md: What does **just distribution** concern?
cards.back_md: The fair sharing of goods and opportunities such as land, schooling and jobs.

cards.front_md: How are **land reforms** and **reserved places** treated here?
cards.back_md: As policies a society may choose; people give reasons on different sides.

cards.front_md: Who wrote **A Theory of Justice**, and when?
cards.back_md: John Rawls, in 1971.

cards.front_md: What is the **original position**?
cards.back_md: An imagined starting point at which people choose the rules of society without knowing their own place.

cards.front_md: What is the **veil of ignorance**?
cards.back_md: The device of choosing rules without knowing one's own future position in society.

cards.front_md: Why would people behind the veil favour fair rules?
cards.back_md: Each might end up in any position, including the worst-off.

cards.front_md: What rules would rational people choose behind the veil?
cards.back_md: Rules that make the worst-off as well off as possible.

cards.front_md: What is the **difference principle**?
cards.back_md: The idea that rules should make the worst-off members of society as well off as possible.

cards.front_md: Where does fairness come from in Rawls' argument?
cards.back_md: From impartial choice, not from altruism.

cards.front_md: What are **minimum basic needs**?
cards.back_md: The basic conditions for a healthy and secure life that a just society should ensure for all.

cards.front_md: Name five **basic needs**
cards.back_md: Adequate nutrition, housing, clean drinking water, education, a minimum wage.

cards.front_md: Two arguments of supporters of **free markets**
cards.back_md: Open competition rewards talent and effort; it gives people choice.

cards.front_md: What do supporters of free markets want the state to do?
cards.back_md: Intervene only minimally.

cards.front_md: Why do some argue for **state intervention**?
cards.back_md: Markets favour those already advantaged, so the state must ensure basic needs and equal opportunity.

cards.front_md: By what means does the state ensure basic needs?
cards.back_md: Public services such as schools, clinics and water supply.

cards.front_md: What do **many societies** do about markets and the state?
cards.back_md: They combine the two.

questions.stem_md: In political theory, the standard meaning of justice is

options.text_md: giving every person exactly the same amount of everything
giving each person what is due to him or her, by fair and accepted principles
giving more to those who already have more
giving whatever the ruler decides

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** giving each person what is due to him or her, by fair and accepted principles. Justice is about giving each person his or her due, treating people fairly by accepted principles. Identical shares for all, extra for the already well off and a ruler's whim are not what the definition describes.

questions.stem_md: A teacher in the imagined town of Hollin tells her class that ideas of justice are very old and found in many traditions. Which list gives correct examples of such traditions or thinkers?

options.text_md: Only modern constitutions written after 1900
Only the ideas of a single thinker of the twentieth century
None, since justice was never discussed before modern times
Dharma in ancient Indian thought, Confucius on just rulers, and Plato's Republic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Dharma in ancient Indian thought, Confucius on just rulers, and Plato's Republic. Dharma, Confucius and Plato's Republic are all long-standing treatments of justice. Justice was discussed long before the twentieth century and not by one thinker alone.

questions.stem_md: The German philosopher Immanuel Kant is linked in this chapter with the idea that

options.text_md: every person has dignity and deserves equal consideration
only citizens of large states have rights
dignity depends on a person's wealth
justice is the interest of the strong

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** every person has dignity and deserves equal consideration. Kant held that every person has dignity and is owed equal consideration. Dignity does not depend on wealth or on the size of one's state, and justice as the interest of the strong is a view that Kant did not share.

questions.stem_md: Which set names the three principles of justice described in this chapter?

options.text_md: Majority rule, seniority, and inheritance
Equal pay, equal wealth, and equal power
Equal treatment for equals, proportionate justice, and recognition of special needs
Tradition, custom, and fashion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Equal treatment for equals, proportionate justice, and recognition of special needs. The three principles are equal treatment for equals, proportionate justice and recognition of special needs. The other sets list ideas that are not the three principles.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Brindle Library charges a lower membership fee to readers of one religion than to readers of another, though all use the same books in the same way. Which principle of justice does this break?

options.text_md: Proportionate justice, since effort is unrewarded
Recognition of special needs, since disability is ignored
Equal treatment for equals, since like persons are treated unlike
None, since libraries may charge what they like

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Equal treatment for equals, since like persons are treated unlike. Readers in the same position are being treated differently because of religion, which breaks equal treatment for equals. No effort or disability is involved, and a free choice of fee does not remove the principle.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Norvale, two workers on a building site get the same daily pay, though one works a double shift of heavy lifting and the other sits and watches. Which principle of justice is most clearly neglected?

options.text_md: Proportionate justice: reward in proportion to effort and the nature of the work
Equal treatment for equals
Recognition of special needs
The veil of ignorance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Proportionate justice: reward in proportion to effort and the nature of the work. Equal pay for very unequal effort ignores proportionate justice. The two workers are not equals in effort, no special need is described, and the veil of ignorance is a method of choosing rules and not a principle of this kind.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Hollin Exam Board gives a wheelchair user extra time and a ground-floor room for an examination. Which principle of justice supports this arrangement?

options.text_md: Proportionate justice, since she works harder
Rule by the majority
Equal treatment, which forbids any difference at all
Recognition of special needs, since a disadvantage may call for special help

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Recognition of special needs, since a disadvantage may call for special help. A disadvantage such as a disability may call for special help so that the person can take part fairly. The case is not about extra effort, majority rule, or a ban on all differences.

questions.stem_md: Under the principle of equal treatment for equals, which of these would a just society avoid?

options.text_md: Rewarding a faster runner with the prize
Refusing a job to a qualified applicant only because of her gender
Giving a ramp to a person who cannot climb steps
Paying more to a person who works longer hours

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Refusing a job to a qualified applicant only because of her gender. Rejecting a qualified person because of gender is discrimination against an equal. Rewarding a faster runner and paying for longer hours reflect proportionate justice, and a ramp reflects special needs.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Vellmark Scholarship Committee has one seat. Asha scored highest in an entrance test, while Dev scored a little lower but has walked four hours each day to study without a school nearby. Giving the seat to Asha stresses one principle, while giving it to Dev stresses another. What does the case best show?

options.text_md: The three principles can pull in different directions, so a society must balance them
Justice has only one correct principle
Special needs never matter in a selection
Equal treatment is the same as proportionate justice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The three principles can pull in different directions, so a society must balance them. Asha's claim rests on reward in proportion to performance, and Dev's rests on disadvantage, so the principles can conflict. A society then balances them with reasons. Justice is not a single principle, and the two are not identical.

questions.stem_md: Social justice is concerned with

options.text_md: the number of seats in a legislature only
the fair distribution of goods and opportunities in a society
the weather and the seasons
the number of roads in a state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the fair distribution of goods and opportunities in a society. Social justice includes the fair distribution of goods and opportunities among members of a society. The other options are not what the term means.

questions.stem_md: Land reforms and reserved places in education and jobs are often given as examples of

options.text_md: rules that every society is bound to adopt
ideas that have no link with distribution
policies that a society may choose in order to change how goods and opportunities are distributed
measures that all thinkers regard in the same way

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** policies that a society may choose in order to change how goods and opportunities are distributed. These are policies a society may choose for the distribution of land or opportunities, and people may hold different views on them. No society is bound to adopt them, they are linked with distribution, and thinkers do not all see them alike.

questions.stem_md: The imagined island of Tamberlay has a few families who hold most of its farmland, while many families farm tiny plots. A council proposes to buy some large holdings and give plots to landless families. Another councillor says the proposal is unfair to those who lose land. Which is the best description of the situation?

options.text_md: It has nothing to do with social justice
It has one answer on which all must agree
It shows that distribution is never a concern of justice
It is a debate about how to distribute a good fairly, in which each side gives reasons

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It is a debate about how to distribute a good fairly, in which each side gives reasons. The question is how a good (land) should be distributed, and both sides give reasons about fairness, so it is a debate within social justice. It is linked with justice, and it does not have a single answer imposed on all.

questions.stem_md: The book A Theory of Justice (1971) was written by

options.text_md: John Stuart Mill
Isaiah Berlin
Immanuel Kant
John Rawls

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** John Rawls. John Rawls wrote A Theory of Justice in 1971. Mill wrote On Liberty, Berlin is linked with negative and positive liberty, and Kant is linked with the idea of human dignity.

questions.stem_md: In Rawls' thought experiment, the veil of ignorance means that people who choose the rules of a society

options.text_md: know exactly how rich they will be
are all rulers of the society
do not know what place they will have in that society
must choose the rules of their own religion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** do not know what place they will have in that society. Behind the veil, people choose rules without knowing their own future position. Knowing one's wealth or ruling status would defeat the purpose of the veil, and religion is not the point.

questions.stem_md: What is the purpose of the original position in Rawls' argument?

options.text_md: To name the first ruler of a country
To imagine a fair starting point where rules are chosen impartially
To list the oldest laws in history
To argue that all people must be equally rich

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To imagine a fair starting point where rules are chosen impartially. The original position is an imagined starting point at which people choose rules without knowing their own place, so that the choice is impartial. It is not about rulers, old laws or equal riches.

questions.stem_md: Before settling on Tamberlay, the imagined islanders agree to decide the rules for sharing fish and land before anyone learns whether he or she will be a boat owner, a net maker or a child of a poor family. This arrangement most closely matches

options.text_md: Rawls' original position behind a veil of ignorance
a decision by the richest family
a system in which each person votes for his or her own benefit alone
rule by the oldest islander

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rawls' original position behind a veil of ignorance. Choosing the rules before knowing one's own place is the idea of the veil of ignorance. A decision by the richest, a vote on known self-interest, and rule by the oldest do not hide a person's future position.

questions.stem_md: Why might people who do not know their future place in society choose fairer rules, according to Rawls?

options.text_md: Because they all become kind by nature
Because they might end up in any position, including the worst-off
Because they dislike all rules
Because the richest people make the rules

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Because they might end up in any position, including the worst-off. Not knowing where one will end up, a rational person would avoid rules that harm those at the bottom, since he or she might be one of them. The argument does not rest on kindness or on rules made by the rich.

questions.stem_md: Behind the veil, the islanders of Tamberlay compare two rule sets. Under Rule Set A, the poorest fifth of islanders gets 20 units of income and the richest fifth gets 130. Under Rule Set B, the poorest fifth gets 40 and the richest fifth gets 90. Which rule set would people reasoning as Rawls describes tend to choose, and why?

options.text_md: Rule Set A, because the richest do better
Either, since the poorest fifth is irrelevant
Neither, because Rawls rejects every rule
Rule Set B, because it leaves the worst-off group better off

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rule Set B, because it leaves the worst-off group better off. People who might land in the worst-off group would prefer the rule set that makes that group as well off as possible, which is Rule Set B (40 against 20). The richest group's gain in Rule Set A is not their concern.

questions.stem_md: A student in the imagined Kesterby Academy says that Rawls' argument works only if people behind the veil are generous. Which reply is correct?

options.text_md: No, the argument rests on impartial choice and rational self-interest, not on altruism
Yes, generosity is the starting point of the argument
No, because Rawls thinks every person is a ruler
Yes, because the veil makes everyone kind

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** No, the argument rests on impartial choice and rational self-interest, not on altruism. The fairness of the rules comes from the impartial choice made without knowing one's own future position, not from kindness. Generosity is not assumed, and the veil does not make people rulers.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is listed among minimum basic needs that a just society should ensure for all?

options.text_md: A luxury car for each household
Free entry to every stadium
Adequate nutrition and clean drinking water
A holiday abroad each year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Adequate nutrition and clean drinking water. Nutrition, housing, clean drinking water, education and a minimum wage are among the basic conditions for a healthy and secure life. Luxury goods and leisure are not basic needs.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Norvale, many families drink from a polluted pond and cannot afford enough food. Which statement best fits the idea of minimum basic needs?

options.text_md: Such matters belong to no one
Only the rich have needs
A just society should see that all have the basic conditions for a healthy life, such as clean water and nutrition
The families should be ignored until the pond dries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A just society should see that all have the basic conditions for a healthy life, such as clean water and nutrition. Clean water and adequate nutrition are basic conditions for a healthy and secure life that a just society should ensure. The other statements deny that need or put it off.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an argument commonly made by supporters of free markets?

options.text_md: Open competition rewards talent and effort and gives people choice
Markets always favour the poor
Government should fix every price
Competition harms everyone equally

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Open competition rewards talent and effort and gives people choice. Supporters hold that competition rewards talent and effort and offers choice, and that minimal state intervention serves people well. Claiming that markets always favour the poor or that the state should fix every price is not their argument.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an argument commonly made by those who favour state intervention?

options.text_md: The state has no role in education
Competition always removes poverty on its own
Public services never help anyone
Markets favour those already advantaged, so the state must ensure basic needs and equal opportunity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Markets favour those already advantaged, so the state must ensure basic needs and equal opportunity. Supporters of intervention hold that markets may favour the already advantaged and that public services can secure basic needs and equal opportunity. The other statements are claims they would reject.

questions.stem_md: Councillor Ravi of the imagined town of Norvale says that the town should let bakers, tailors and carters compete freely, because competition rewards effort and gives buyers a choice. His view is closest to

options.text_md: the argument for the state to run every shop
the argument for free markets with minimal intervention
the view that effort never matters
the view that choice is harmful

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the argument for free markets with minimal intervention. Reward for effort, competition and choice are the central claims of the free market view. State management of every shop and the rejection of effort or choice are different positions.

questions.stem_md: Councillor Meera of the imagined town of Kesterby says that poor children there cannot compete fairly with others unless the town runs free schools and clinics. Her view is closest to

options.text_md: the argument for state intervention through public services
the argument that the market will always supply schools
the argument that nothing can help
the argument for no public service

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the argument for state intervention through public services. Providing free schools and clinics so that all have a fair chance is the state intervention view. The other options reject public provision or say that nothing helps.

questions.stem_md: The imagined island of Tamberlay lets private traders sell goods freely, but it also runs a public water supply and a school for every village. How is this arrangement best described?

options.text_md: A pure free market with no state role
A combination of markets and state action, as many societies adopt
A system in which the state controls everything
A system with neither market nor state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A combination of markets and state action, as many societies adopt. Free trade alongside public water and schools combines market and state, as many societies do. It is not a pure market, nor state control of all things.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Hollin Council sets a minimum daily wage for workers in its brick kilns. A kiln owner says this interferes with free bargaining, while a union leader says that workers with no choice would otherwise be paid too little for a secure life. This disagreement is best described as

options.text_md: a case on which all thinkers agree
a matter outside social justice
a debate between a market view and a state intervention view
an example of the veil of ignorance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a debate between a market view and a state intervention view. The owner stresses free bargaining and the union leader stresses securing a basic need through state action, which is the market versus intervention debate. The disagreement is not outside social justice, and no veil is involved.

questions.stem_md: A student of the imagined Brindle School must write on markets and state intervention. Which approach best fits a balanced answer?

options.text_md: Praise one view and ignore the other
List only names of thinkers
Say that all societies must adopt the same approach
State the reasons of both views and then give a reasoned judgement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** State the reasons of both views and then give a reasoned judgement. A balanced answer sets out each view with its reasons and then judges. Praising one side, listing names or saying that all must follow a single approach is not balanced.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Vellmark Committee gives some scholarships by test score and some by family hardship. Which statement best evaluates this mixed approach?

options.text_md: It is unjust because any mix is wrong
It shows that justice has no principles
It applies the same principle to everyone
It tries to balance reward for performance with recognition of disadvantage, though people may disagree on the right mix

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It tries to balance reward for performance with recognition of disadvantage, though people may disagree on the right mix. A mix of score-based and need-based awards weighs proportionate justice and special needs together, and reasonable people may differ over the proportion. It is not wrong in itself, and it does not show a lack of principles or a single principle.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Norvale, a free market sets the price of grain. In a drought the price doubles and poor families cannot afford enough. One thinker says the market should be left alone, another says the state should supply grain at a fixed low price to the poor. What is the best conclusion?

options.text_md: Only the first thinker may speak
The case has no link with basic needs
The case sets the reasons for free markets against those for state action to secure a basic need
Both thinkers want the same thing in the same way

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The case sets the reasons for free markets against those for state action to secure a basic need. One stresses market operation and the other stresses securing a basic need through the state, so both views are in play. The case concerns basic needs, and the thinkers differ in approach.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Rawls holds that rules chosen behind a veil of ignorance are likely to be fair.

**Reason (R):** People who do not know their future place in society cannot shape the rules to favour their own position.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: when no one knows where he or she will stand, the rules cannot be tilted toward a known position, which makes them impartial.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Justice is commonly defined as giving each person his or her due.

**Reason (R):** Justice requires that every person receive exactly the same reward whatever the effort.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: proportionate justice holds that reward should reflect effort, skill and the nature of the work, so identical rewards are not required.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Recognition of special needs is one of the three principles of justice.

**Reason (R):** Proportionate justice means rewarding people in proportion to their effort and skill.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: R describes a different principle, and special needs are recognised because of disadvantage, not because of effort.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Rawls' argument, fair rules come mainly from the kindness of the people who choose them.

**Reason (R):** In his argument, fairness comes from an impartial choice made without knowledge of one's own future position.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the argument does not depend on kindness. R is true and gives the actual source of fairness, so it contradicts A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Some supporters of free markets favour minimal state intervention.

**Reason (R):** They argue that open competition rewards talent and effort and offers people choice.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: if competition itself rewards effort and offers choice, there is less reason for the state to intervene.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Some thinkers argue that the state must provide public services for basic needs.

**Reason (R):** They hold that markets may favour those who are already advantaged, leaving others without the conditions for a secure life.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: if markets can favour the already advantaged, public services become a way to secure basic needs and equal opportunity.

questions.stem_md: Proportionate justice holds that a society should pay the same wage to every person, whatever work is done and however much effort is made.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Proportionate justice holds that rewards should be in proportion to effort, skill and the nature of the work, so it does not support identical pay for all.

questions.stem_md: Equal treatment for equals means that people should not be discriminated against on grounds such as caste, religion or gender.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Equal treatment for equals requires equal rights and no discrimination on such grounds.

questions.stem_md: In the veil of ignorance argument, the people who choose the rules are told in advance exactly which group of society they will belong to.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** They are not told. The veil means that they choose without knowing their own future place, and this is why the choice is impartial.

questions.stem_md: Many societies combine some features of free markets with some state action, instead of using only one approach.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Many societies combine the two, using markets for much of the economy and public services for basic needs.

questions.stem_md: Justice means giving each person his or her ___.
questions.solution_md: Justice means giving each person what is due to him or her.

questions.stem_md: John Rawls' idea that people choose rules without knowing their own future place is called the veil of ___, and the imagined starting point is the ___ position.
questions.solution_md: The idea is the veil of ignorance, and the imagined starting point is the original position.

questions.stem_md: A just society should ensure that everyone has the minimum basic ___ for a healthy and secure life.
questions.solution_md: Minimum basic needs, such as nutrition, housing and clean drinking water, should be ensured for all.

questions.stem_md: Match each principle of justice with the situation in the imagined town of Hollin that it best supports.

options.text_md: Equal treatment for equals
Proportionate justice
Recognition of special needs
Veil of ignorance

match_right.text_md: A mason who builds three walls is paid more than one who builds one wall
Rules are chosen by people who do not know their own future place
Every qualified applicant is judged by the same rules whatever his or her caste or gender
A child who cannot see is given books in a form she can read

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Equal rules for all qualified applicants match equal treatment, more pay for more work matches proportion, books for a child who cannot see match special needs, and choosing rules without knowing one's place is the veil.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined statement from a debate in Kesterby with the position it expresses.

options.text_md: Let sellers compete, and the best will win custom
The town must run a school for children who cannot pay
Competition rewards effort, but a public water supply serves the basic need of all
A person must be able to afford food before any choice has meaning

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Competition for custom is the free market view, a free school is state intervention, competition along with public water is a combination, and food before choice is the basic needs argument.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the veil of ignorance argument as the imagined islanders of Tamberlay might reason.

options.text_md: Rules that leave the worst-off as well off as possible are likely to be chosen
Suppose that no one knows what place he or she will hold in it
Each person asks which rules would be acceptable whichever place he or she gets
Imagine that all people are to choose the rules of society

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The thought experiment begins with a choice of rules, adds the veil, asks which rules one would accept from any place, and ends with rules that serve the worst-off well.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in a sensible order for a committee in the imagined town of Brindle that must award one scholarship fairly.

options.text_md: Consider any special disadvantage and give reasons for the final choice
Consider the effort and performance of each applicant
Check that all applicants who are equals are treated alike
State the principles that the committee will apply

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). The committee first states its principles, then checks equal treatment, then weighs performance, then considers special need and gives its reasons.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is meant by justice? Name one tradition or thinker that has discussed it.
questions.solution_md: Definition and a tradition.

answer.model_answer_md: **Justice** means giving each person what is **due** to him or her, treating people fairly by accepted principles. It has been discussed in many traditions, for example **dharma** in ancient Indian thought or Plato's **Republic**.

marking_scheme.step: Giving each person his or her due, fairly

questions.stem_md: Name the three principles of justice and state any one of them briefly.
questions.solution_md: Three names, one explained.

answer.model_answer_md: The three principles are **equal treatment for equals**, **proportionate justice** and **recognition of special needs**. For example, proportionate justice holds that rewards should be in **proportion** to effort and skill.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Hollin, a village school builds a ramp and gives a blind pupil audio books. Which principle of justice does this follow, and why?
questions.solution_md: Principle and reason.

answer.model_answer_md: It follows **recognition of special needs**. A person with a disadvantage, such as a disability, may need **special treatment** so that he or she can take part on fair terms with others.

marking_scheme.step: Disadvantage may need special help to take part fairly

questions.stem_md: Explain in two sentences what Rawls meant by the veil of ignorance.
questions.solution_md: Idea and its effect.

answer.model_answer_md: The **veil of ignorance** is an imagined situation in which people choose the rules of society **without knowing** what place they will hold in it. Because they might be anyone, they must choose rules that are **fair** to all.

marking_scheme.step: Choosing rules without knowing one's future place
The result is fair rules, since anyone could be affected

questions.stem_md: According to Rawls, what kind of rules would rational people behind the veil choose, and why?
questions.solution_md: Rules for the worst-off, with the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: They would choose rules that leave the **worst-off** as well off as possible. Since a person might end up in the **worst position**, each would want it to be as good as possible.

marking_scheme.step: Rules that make the worst-off as well off as possible
Each might end up in the worst position

questions.stem_md: What does social justice say about the distribution of goods and opportunities? Give one example of a policy a society may choose.
questions.solution_md: Fair distribution and an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Social justice is concerned with the **fair distribution** of goods and opportunities in a society. A society may choose policies such as **land reforms** or reserved places in education and jobs.

marking_scheme.step: Fair distribution of goods and opportunities
An example of a policy a society may choose

questions.stem_md: What are minimum basic needs? Name any three.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and three examples.

answer.model_answer_md: **Minimum basic needs** are the basic conditions for a healthy and secure life that a just society should ensure for all. Examples are **adequate nutrition**, **housing**, **clean drinking water**, education and a minimum wage.

marking_scheme.step: Basic conditions for a healthy, secure life

questions.stem_md: State two reasons given by supporters of free markets.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Supporters argue that **open competition** rewards talent and effort. They also say that markets give people **choice** and generally serve people well, so the state should intervene only a little.

marking_scheme.step: Choice, and generally serving people well

questions.stem_md: Why do some thinkers argue that the state must intervene to pursue social justice?
questions.solution_md: Markets may favour the advantaged; the state secures needs.

answer.model_answer_md: They argue that **markets favour** those who are already advantaged. So the state must ensure **basic needs** and **equal opportunity** through public services such as schools and clinics.

marking_scheme.step: Markets may favour the already advantaged
The state should ensure basic needs and equal opportunity through public services

questions.stem_md: Two islanders of imagined Tamberlay decide the rules of fishing before they know whether they will own boats or not. Name the idea and say why such a choice may be fair.
questions.solution_md: Idea and reason.

answer.model_answer_md: This is the **original position behind a veil of ignorance**. Each person might own a boat or not, so each must choose rules that are **fair** to both, and the choice is **impartial**.

marking_scheme.step: Original position behind a veil of ignorance
Impartial choice because one's place is unknown

questions.stem_md: Explain, with an example, how the three principles of justice can conflict and how a society may balance them.
questions.solution_md: Conflict, example, balance.

answer.model_answer_md: The principles may conflict. A **reward in proportion to performance** may favour the best scorer, while **special needs** may favour a person with a disadvantage, and **equal treatment** asks that equals be treated alike. A society may **balance** them by stating its principles, giving reasons, and using a mix, such as awards for both merit and hardship.

marking_scheme.step: Principles may conflict, with an example
A society balances them with reasons or a mix

questions.stem_md: The imagined islanders of Tamberlay compare two rule sets for sharing income. Explain why people behind a veil of ignorance might prefer the set that gives the poorest group 40 units over the one that gives it 20, even if the richest group gets less.
questions.solution_md: Veil, worst-off, rational preference.

answer.model_answer_md: Behind the **veil**, no one knows his or her place, so each might belong to the **poorest group**. A rational person would therefore prefer the rule set that makes that group **better off**, namely 40 rather than 20, even if the **richest group** receives less. The choice rests on impartial reasoning.

marking_scheme.step: No one knows his or her place
Each might be in the poorest group, so prefer 40 to 20

questions.stem_md: Does Rawls' argument depend on people being generous? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Fairness from impartiality, not altruism.

answer.model_answer_md: No. The argument rests on **impartial choice**. People behind the **veil of ignorance** do not know their own future position, so a rational person chooses rules that would be **acceptable from any position**. Fairness comes from the method of choosing and not from **altruism**.

marking_scheme.step: Answer: no, the argument does not rest on generosity
People do not know their future position

questions.stem_md: Present the views of supporters of free markets and of state intervention on how to ensure basic needs, without taking a side.
questions.solution_md: Both views and the combination.

answer.model_answer_md: Some argue that **free markets** reward talent and effort and give people choice, with minimal state intervention. Others argue that markets **favour the already advantaged**, so the state must ensure **basic needs** and equal opportunity through public services. Many societies **combine** the two.

marking_scheme.step: Free market view with a reason
State intervention view with a reason

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Hollin, many families lack clean water, and school places are few. Explain how this relates to minimum basic needs and suggest one way each of a market view and a state view might respond.
questions.solution_md: Basic needs and two responses.

answer.model_answer_md: Clean water and **education** are among the **minimum basic needs** that a just society should ensure. A market view might favour **private suppliers** competing to sell water and run schools. A state view might favour a **public water supply** and free schools funded by the town.

marking_scheme.step: Water and education as basic needs

questions.stem_md: The imagined Vellmark Scholarship Committee must choose between a top scorer who is well off and a slightly lower scorer who lives far from any school. Show how the three principles of justice apply.
questions.solution_md: Three principles applied.

answer.model_answer_md: **Equal treatment** asks that both be judged by the same rules. **Proportionate justice** supports the top scorer, since reward follows performance. **Recognition of special needs** supports the other, since distance is a disadvantage. The committee should give **reasons** for how it balances them.

marking_scheme.step: Proportionate justice and special needs on opposite sides

questions.stem_md: Explain why social justice includes the fair distribution of goods and opportunities, and how land reforms or reservations are treated in such a discussion.
questions.solution_md: Distribution, fairness, policies as choices.

answer.model_answer_md: A society has limited **goods and opportunities**, such as land, schooling and jobs, so how they are **distributed** affects people's lives. Social justice asks whether that distribution is **fair**. Land reforms and reservations are **policies a society may choose**, and people hold **different views** and give reasons.

marking_scheme.step: Goods and opportunities are limited and their distribution matters
Social justice asks whether the distribution is fair
Land reforms and reservations are policies a society may choose; views differ

questions.stem_md: Explain the three principles of justice, and say how they can conflict.
questions.solution_md: Three principles, a conflict and balance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Equal treatment for equals** gives people in like positions the same rights, with no discrimination by caste, religion or gender.
2. **Proportionate justice** ties the reward to what a person puts in: effort, skill and the kind of work done.
3. **Recognition of special needs**: people with disadvantages, such as a disability, may need special help.
4. The principles can **conflict**: one scholarship may suit a top scorer or a person in hardship.
5. A society **balances** them, with reasons and a mix of measures.

questions.stem_md: Explain Rawls' idea of the veil of ignorance and the original position, and say why he thinks it leads to fair rules.
questions.solution_md: Book, original position, veil, rules for the worst-off, impartial choice.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. John Rawls' book **A Theory of Justice** (1971) puts forward a thought experiment.
2. In the **original position**, people choose the rules of society.
3. A **veil of ignorance** hides from them their future place in society.
4. Since each might end up as the **worst-off**, rational people would choose rules that make the worst-off as well off as possible.
5. Fairness comes from **impartial choice**, not from altruism.

marking_scheme.step: Rawls and A Theory of Justice (1971)
Rules that make the worst-off as well off as possible
Fairness from impartial choice, not altruism

questions.stem_md: Explain the idea of justice with reference to different traditions and to the idea of dignity, and say how social justice concerns distribution.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, traditions, dignity and distribution.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Justice** means giving each person his or her **due**, treating people fairly by accepted principles.
2. It has been discussed in many traditions: **dharma** in ancient Indian thought, **Confucius** on just rulers, and Plato's **Republic**.
3. **Kant** saw **dignity** in every person, so each is owed equal consideration.
4. **Social justice** asks whether goods and opportunities are shared fairly among people.
5. Land reforms or reservations are policies a society may choose, and people give reasons on different sides.

marking_scheme.step: Policies a society may choose, views differing

questions.stem_md: A just society should ensure minimum basic needs. Discuss the views on free markets and on state intervention as ways of pursuing this, giving reasons for each.
questions.solution_md: Basic needs, both views with reasons, and combination.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Minimum basic needs** are nutrition, housing, clean drinking water, education and a minimum wage.
2. Some argue for **free markets**: open competition rewards talent and effort and gives choice.
3. They favour minimal **state intervention**, and hold that markets generally serve people well.
4. Others argue that markets **favour the advantaged**, so the state must secure basic needs and equal opportunity through public services.
5. Many societies **combine** the two, and students should judge with reasons.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined island of Tamberlay, a few families own most of the farmland and many own none. Using ideas on just distribution and basic needs, explain how islanders might discuss what is fair, and what policies may be chosen.
questions.solution_md: Distribution, basic needs, policy choice, both views, combination.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Social justice concerns the **fair distribution** of goods and opportunities, and land is one such good.
2. Islanders may ask whether the distribution gives all the **basic conditions** for a secure life.
3. A policy such as **land reform** is one that a society may choose, with reasons on different sides.
4. Supporters of **markets** may stress effort and choice, while supporters of **state action** may stress basic needs and equal opportunity.
5. They might **combine** measures and give reasons.

marking_scheme.step: Fair distribution of goods such as land
A policy a society may choose

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the statement: a just society treats all alike. Use the three principles of justice, the veil of ignorance and the debate on markets and the state.
questions.solution_md: A weighed answer using all ideas.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Equal treatment** supports the statement for equals, with no discrimination.
2. But **proportionate justice** rewards effort differently, and **special needs** may call for different help.
3. Behind the **veil of ignorance**, people might choose rules that make the worst-off as well off as possible.
4. Some favour **markets** and others favour **state action**, and many combine them.
5. So a reasoned judgement is that justice means treating equals alike and others according to relevant differences.

marking_scheme.step: Proportion and special needs qualify the statement
